cat=cs.CL url=https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12004v1
s[0] Understanding the Effectiveness of Very Large Language Models on Dialog Evaluation Very Large Language Models for Dialog Evaluation J.
s[1] Huynh et al.
s[2] Jessica Huynh Carnegie Mellon University, jhuynh@cs.cmu.edu Cathy Jiao Carnegie Mellon University, cljiao@cs.cmu.edu Prakhar Gupta Carnegie Mellon University, prakharg@cs.cmu.edu Shikib Mehri Amazon, asmehri@amazon.com (work done while at Carnegie Mellon University) Payal Bajaj Microsoft Turing, pabajaj@microsoft.com Vishrav Chaudhary Microsoft Turing,
s[3] vchaudhary@microsoft.com Maxine Eskenazi Carnegie Mellon University, max@cs.cmu.edu * Jessica Huynh, Cathy Jiao, Prakhar Gupta, Shikib Mehri, Payal Bajaj, Vishrav Chaudhary, Maxine Eskenazi January 14, 2024 =========================================================================================================== Language models have steadily increased in size over the past few years.
s[4] They achieve a high level of performance on various natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as question answering and summarization.
s[5] Large language models (LLMs) have been used for generation and can now output human-like text.
s[6] Due to this, there are other downstream tasks in the realm of dialog that can now harness the LLMs' language understanding capabilities.
s[7] Dialog evaluation is one task that this paper will explore.
s[8] It concentrates on prompting with LLMs: BLOOM, OPT, GPT-3, Flan-T5, InstructDial and TNLGv2.
s[9] The paper shows that the choice of datasets used for training a model contributes to how well it performs on a task as well as on how the prompt should be structured.
s[10] Specifically, the more diverse and relevant the group of datasets that a model is trained on, the better dialog evaluation performs.
s[11] This paper also investigates how the number of examples in the prompt and the type of example selection used affect the model's performance.
s[12] § INTRODUCTION In recent years, language models such as GPT-3 <cit.> have grown larger, and their performance on downstream natural language processing (NLP) tasks has significantly improved in low-resource settings where only a few instances per task are available (few-shot).
s[13] The larger these models are, the higher their performances trend on tasks such as language generation and evaluation <cit.>.
s[14] They can generate coherent, fluent and interesting responses.
s[15] However, they can also produce responses that are repetitive and un-engaging <cit.>, in addition to being hard to control.

READ 2303.15078v3 | Large Language Models are Diverse Role-Players for Summarization Evaluation
cat=cs.CL url=https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.15078v3
s[0] N.
s[1] Wu et al.
s[2] STCA Search & Distribution Group, Microsoft, China wuning,migon,lisho,shiningliang,djiang@microsoft.com Large Language Models are Diverse Role-Players for Summarization Evaluation Ning Wu Ming GongCorresponding author.
s[3] Linjun Shou Shining Liang Daxin Jiang ================================================================================ Text summarization has a wide range of applications in many scenarios.
s[4] The evaluation of the quality of the generated text is a complex problem.
s[5] A big challenge to language evaluation is that there is a clear divergence between existing metrics and human evaluation.
s[6] A document summary’s quality can be assessed by human annotators on various criteria, both objective ones like grammar and correctness, and subjective ones like informativeness, succinctness, and appeal.
s[7] Most of the automatic evaluation methods like BLUE/ROUGE may be not able to adequately capture the above dimensions.
s[8] In this paper, we propose a new evaluation framework based on LLMs, which provides a comprehensive evaluation framework by comparing generated text and reference text from both objective and subjective aspects.
s[9] First, we propose to model objective and subjective dimensions of generated text based on roleplayers prompting mechanism.
s[10] Furthermore, we introduce a context-based prompting mechanism that is able to generate dynamic roleplayer profiles based on input context.
s[11] Finally, we design a multi-roleplayer prompting technology based on batch prompting and integrate multiple outputs into the final evaluation results.
s[12] Experimental results on three real datasets for summarization show that our model is highly competitive and has a very high consistency with human annotators.
s[13] § INTRODUCTION Text summarization has wide applications in various research and application fields.
s[14] Recently, some works found that there is a clear gap between existed metrics like BLEU <cit.>, ROUGE, BertScore <cit.> and human annotations <cit.>.
s[15] Although typical overlap-based and model-based metrics can capture lexicon level or semantic level similarity between generated text and reference text, specific dimensions like coherence, grammar, and interestingness still can't be captured.

s[1] 2024 ================================================================================================================================================================================================== In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained significant popularity due to their ability to generate human-like text and their potential applications in various fields,
s[2] such as Software Engineering.
s[3] LLMs for Code are commonly trained on large unsanitized corpora of source code scraped from the Internet.
s[4] The content of these datasets is memorized and emitted by the models, often in a verbatim manner.
s[5] In this work, we will discuss the security, privacy, and licensing implications of memorization.
s[6] We argue why the use of copyleft code to train LLMs is a legal and ethical dilemma.
s[7] Finally, we provide four actionable recommendations to address this issue.
s[8] § LANGUAGE MODELS FOR CODE Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained significant attention in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP) in recent years due to their ability to perform a wide range of NLP tasks with impressive accuracy.
s[9] These models, trained on massive amounts of data, improve in accuracy as they grow from millions to billions of parameters.
s[10] LLMs for code are trained on massive amounts of data and can learn the structure and syntax of programming languages, making them well-suited for tasks such as code summarization, generation, and completion <cit.>.
s[11] LLMs are even making their way into commercial products like GitHub's Copilot, Replits's GhostWriter and Tabnine.
s[12] Meanwhile, some have identified that LLMs can memorize large swaths of training data  <cit.>.
s[13] Memorization enables the extraction of the data using Data Extraction Attacks.
s[14] Some attacks have even been able to extract addresses and other personal information from public models <cit.>.
s[15] Memorization also impacts LLMs for code, with all its associated consequences.

# Large Language Model Evaluation Methods

Large Language Models (LLMs) have become increasingly popular in recent years, with applications ranging from software engineering to natural language processing. Evaluating LLMs is crucial for ensuring their reliability and effectiveness. This brief outlines the main evaluation methods used in recent years, focusing on both the objects being evaluated and the reliability of the evaluations.
